extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy; merchants, lawmakers, and policymakers interested in money, trade, and public finance
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from a classical political-economy treatise discussing the nature of wealth, the role of money and bullion, balance of trade, and the practical consequences for commerce and public finance. It offers normative claims about what governments and merchants should or should not pursue regarding money and trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wealth defined by consumable goods (not money)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wealth does not consist in money, or in gold and silver, but in what money purchases; money is valuable only for purchasing goods and services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that money is only part of national capital and generally the most unprofitable part; compares attempting to increase gold to forcing families to hoard unnecessary kitchen utensils — it diminishes the real wealth that feeds, clothes, and lodges people. Argues that attempting to increase wealth by accumulating unnecessary bullion will reduce the wealth devoted to consumable goods and productive uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Money as the measure of value and instrument of commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: Money serves as the common measure by which we estimate the value of all other commodities and is the established instrument of commerce for which other things are readily exchanged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains common language uses (a rich man "worth" money), and gives ethnographic examples (Tartars measuring wealth in cattle). Emphasizes that money's primary function is to facilitate exchange and to be the thing for which other commodities are readily given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government should not prioritize accumulating or preserving bullion
rubrics_metrics.description: The attention of government is unnecessarily and mistakenly directed toward preserving or increasing the quantity of money (gold and silver) in the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that free trade will supply gold and silver in proportion to what a country can afford; that money quantity is regulated by effectual demand; that prohibitions and policies aimed at hoarding bullion are fruitless and often counterproductive. Gives historical policy examples (Spain, Portugal, Scotland) and criticizes their effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of trade drives international bullion flows
rubrics_metrics.description: When a country exports more in value than it imports, it becomes due a balance from foreigners which is paid in gold and silver and thus increases domestic bullion; the reverse reduces bullion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides an explicit mechanism and numerical example (exchange five percent against England: 105 ounces in England buys bill for 100 ounces in Holland) showing how exchange rates affect which country gains or loses bullion. Uses this to explain why worrying about bullion exportation alone is misplaced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibitions on bullion exportation are ineffective and often harmful
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws forbidding the export of gold and silver cannot prevent exportation when private parties have advantage in doing so, and such prohibitions make smuggling more dangerous and expensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples of restrictive laws (Spain, Portugal, old Scotch acts) show they are circumvented; merchants argued prohibitions increase exchange costs and make foreign payments heavier, thus worsening the trade balance rather than improving it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exporting bullion to buy foreign goods can increase national treasure via re-exports
rubrics_metrics.description: Sending gold or silver abroad to buy foreign goods may increase the country's bullion if those goods are profitably re-exported or sold abroad, bringing back more treasure than was sent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites merchants' argument and Mr. Mun's seed-and-harvest analogy: initial outlay (exported bullion) can yield larger returns through trade if the goods are re-exported at profit. Recognized as partly solid reasoning in certain commercial contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity of money regulated by effectual demand and ease of transport
rubrics_metrics.description: The quantity of any commodity, including gold and silver, naturally regulates itself according to effectual demand — the demand of those willing to pay the full cost of bringing it to market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that because gold and silver are small in bulk and highly valuable they can be transported easily from places where they are cheap to places where they are dear, so supply adjusts to demand (contrast with bulkier commodities like grain). Gives examples comparing importing gold versus grain in terms of shipping requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Price stability of gold and silver due to transportability
rubrics_metrics.description: Because gold and silver can be transported easily from where they are abundant to where they are scarce, their price does not fluctuate as violently as that of bulkier commodities; changes are generally slow, gradual, and uniform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that large sudden changes in the money price of all other commodities require major commercial revolutions (e.g., discovery of America). Acknowledges some long-term decline in value of metals in Europe due to continual importations, but stresses general stability relative to other goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scarcity of money often reflects credit shortages and over-trading
rubrics_metrics.description: Complaints of scarcity of money frequently result not from a true dearth of gold and silver but from over-trading and the inability of traders to borrow or convert goods into money in time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how sober merchants can suffer when projects exceed capital (over-trading), leading to increased demand for money before returns arrive; lenders refuse loans and debtors can't pay, producing perceived scarcity even when bullion exists in the economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Barter, credit, and well-regulated paper money can substitute for bullion
rubrics_metrics.description: If gold and silver fall short, barter, credit arrangements, and properly regulated paper money can supply the functions of money with varying degrees of inconvenience or advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details mechanisms: barter and periodic clearing of credits, buying and selling on credit, and the potential advantages of well-regulated paper-money. Suggests these are preferable to obsessive accumulation of bullion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gold and silver are durable utensils but unproductive components of capital
rubrics_metrics.description: Gold and silver (as coin or plate) are utensils used to circulate commodities and for display, but they are the least productive part of national capital and cannot serve other productive purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compares bullion and plate to kitchen utensils: accumulating more than the use requires is absurd and will diminish wealth used for consumption and productive labor; plate is regulated by private taste and will expand with private wealth but hoarded bullion is wasted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign wars and large external expenses are funded chiefly by exports and annual produce, not by hoarded bullion
rubrics_metrics.description: Nations sustain expensive wars mainly from annual produce, exports of commodities, and public borrowing, rather than by melting down private plate or exporting circulating bullion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses British wartime finance as example: huge wartime expenses were met largely by exporting British commodities, contracting debt, and other financial instruments rather than by shipping away the country's circulating coin or private plate. Describes three ways to pay foreign armies: accumulated treasure, manufactures, or rude produce, with emphasis on the last two being primary.

rubrics_metrics.name: International bullion (bullion-in-transit) functions as the money of the mercantile republic
rubrics_metrics.description: Bullion that is alternately imported and exported among commercial countries circulates as the money of the international mercantile system, distinct from each nation's domestic circulating coin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that this international money adjusts its movement according to trade and war (e.g., circulating more about the seat of war) and that whatever part a nation uses must have been acquired by commodities or things purchased with them — ultimately tying back to a country's annual produce.
